To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the decision to idle a rig depends on its age and the age and size of the drilling contractor that owns it; (2) the decision to reactivate a rig depends on the rig's age, the age of its owner, the age of the owner's other rigs, and the size of the owner; and (3) the idling and reactivation decisions are not made independently of each other.

(1) drilling contractors idled and reactivated rigs in response to changes (increases and decreases) in oil prices; (2) drilling contractors idling and reactivation decisions were driven in large part by the characteristics of the rig being idled or reactivated, including its location, size, and type; (3) drilling contractors' idling and re-activation decisions were also driven in part by the characteristics and strategies of the firm idling or reactivating the rig, including

(i) the decision to idle a rig depends on the rig's productivity, the firm's financial strength, the firm's market position, and the level of the rig's utilization, (ii) the decision to reactivate a rig depends on its productivity, the firm that owns it, and the level at which it is reactivated, and (iii) the level of utilization at which a rig is idled depends on its productivity and the firm that owns the rig.

how firms make capacity decisions when demand for their product fluctuates.
the idling and reactivation of offshore drilling rigs.
the strategic interaction between oil and gas companies and drilling contractors in the offshore drilling market.
